ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A uniform electric field with a horizontal direction (as shown in the figure). A small positively charged ball with mass \( m \) starts from point \( O \) with an initial velocity of magnitude \( v_{0} \). Under the action of the electric force and gravity, it moves precisely along a straight line at an angle \( \theta \) to the opposite direction of the electric field.

1. What is the difference in electric potential energy of the small ball when it reaches the highest point compared to its electric potential energy at point $O$?

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: A uniform electric field with a horizontal direction (as shown in the figure). A small positively charged ball with mass \( m \) starts from point \( O \) with an initial velocity of magnitude \( v_{0} \). Under the action of the electric force and gravity, it moves precisely along a straight line at an angle \( \theta \) to the opposite direction of the electric field. What is the difference in electric potential energy of the small ball when it reaches the highest point compared to its electric potential energy at point \( O \)?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there are multiple horizontal uniform electric field lines, with arrows pointing to the left, labeled E; the small ball starts from point O, with initial velocity v0 along an oblique line toward the upper right, and the angle between the oblique line and the horizontally rightward direction is θ. Horizontally rightward is exactly the opposite direction of the electric field direction. Reasoning: The small ball is positively charged, the magnitude of the electric field force is qE and the direction is to the left, and the direction of gravity mg is downward. The problem states that the small ball still moves along the oblique straight line where the initial velocity is located under the action of these two constant forces, so the resultant force must be along the opposite direction of the line of motion, namely toward the lower left, and correspond to the angle θ with the horizontal. Therefore there is mg/qE = tanθ, equivalently qE = mg cotθ. At the highest point, the vertical velocity is 0. The initial vertical component of velocity is v0 sinθ, and the vertical acceleration is -g, so the vertical rising height h = (v0 sinθ)^2/(2g) = v0^2 sin^2θ/(2g). Since the trajectory is a straight line with angle θ to the horizontal, the horizontally rightward displacement x = h/tanθ = v0^2 sinθ cosθ/(2g). The electric field is to the left, and the small ball moves to the right, that is, it moves against the electric field direction, so the increase in electric potential energy is ΔU_e = qE x. Substituting qE = mg cotθ and x gives ΔU_e = mg cotθ · v0^2 sinθ cosθ/(2g) = (1/2)m v0^2 cos^2θ.
